text: MORNING MARKET BRIEF Monday, August 10, 2026  TL;DR  1/ The regime shifts from Fragile to Coiled: long gamma dealer positioning, closing weakness window, and accelerating buybacks are building coiled energy, but the setup is fragile ahead of Wednesday's CPI.  2/ Hormuz is not resolved -- the Iran-Oman deal is a traffic management workaround, Tehran's real demands are nowhere near the table, and weekend missile and drone strikes on refinery infrastructure keep the energy risk premium structurally alive.  3/ A hot CPI reignites oil-driven inflation anxiety and is the single most likely catalyst to flip the read back toward Fragile; that's the number to watch this week.  4/ Lean long on dips in the 7600-7800 SPX range using the corporate bid and closing weakness window as your anchor, but size conservatively into the print.  5/ Meta's Muse Glimmer is a direct shot at closed-model incumbents and structurally pressures the monetization assumptions holding up high-multiple AI pure-plays.  KEY THEMES  Geopolitics and macro are beginning to reassert themselves as the dominant pricing forces just as earnings season fades, and that intersection is most acute in the energy complex, where Hormuz remains structurally unresolved despite weekend headlines about an Iran-Oman navigation deal. That agreement, if finalized, addresses maritime traffic management, not the blockade itself; the conditions Iran is demanding for full Strait reopening -- sanctions relief, troop withdrawal, war-damage compensation -- are nowhere near the table, and the appointment of hardliner Mohsen Rezaei to head the Supreme National Security Council signals Tehran is playing for lasting leverage, not an exit ramp. With a tanker struck by anti-ship missile off Oman yesterday and drone attacks hitting both Saudi and Russian refinery infrastructure over the weekend, the geopolitical risk premium in crude is not going away. Wednesday's US CPI print -- now the focal point for Fed rate path expectations after Friday's surprise payroll contraction pushed September hike odds down to ~45% -- will determine whether oil-driven inflation anxiety forces the hand of a Fed already internally fractured. Meanwhile, the equity structure remains range-bound and gamma-pinned between 7600 and 7800 on SPX, with systematic flows offering little incremental buying power this week; the asymmetry favors the downside in the event of a vol shock, but the re-acceleration of corporate buybacks as blackout windows lift should cushion any near-term dip and keep the tape from breaking sharply ahead of the data.  MARKET SNAPSHOT  The macro tape is coalescing around Wednesday's CPI print as the fulcrum event for the week: Friday's soft payrolls halved near-term hike probability to ~45% and drove Treasuries higher, but 10-year yields have since stabilized at 4.65% and the dollar is edging back, suggesting the market isn't ready to fully price out tightening risk ahead of the inflation data. JPMorgan raising their S&P 500 year-end target to 8,000 on AI earnings momentum adds a fundamental anchor to the current record-level tape, but with earnings largely behind us, Hormuz and CPI are the two variables that can reprice both oil and rate expectations simultaneously.  MACRO  USD/JPY at 158.85 -- 400 pips off the post-intervention low of ~155 -- illustrates the structural limits of coordinated intervention when the rate differential, fiscal trajectory, and geopolitical risk premium driving yen weakness remain entirely unaddressed. With Japan entering the Obon holiday period and Tuesday's session thinned by the domestic holiday, liquidity conditions are ripe for another intervention episode, but any resulting yen rally should be treated as a tactical opportunity rather than a trend reversal absent a genuine Fed pivot or BOJ policy shift.  China PPI printing at -3.5% YoY / -0.7% MoM came as no surprise given that the July manufacturing PMI output prices sub-index had already signaled the miss at 47.8, but the confirmation matters: with credit impulse at its weakest since 2008, the pipeline points to persistent and deepening factory-gate disinflation, which adds structural downward pressure on global goods inflation and complicates the reflation trade in EM commodity exporters exposed to Chinese industrial demand.  CORPORATE  Berkshire's profit doubling on investment gains and industrial/retail strength reinforces the view that old-economy earnings remain resilient even as AI-sector volatility persists; the broad premarket bid in semis (AMAT, MRVL, INTC, SMC) reflects continued sector risk appetite despite recent chop, while the Trump-backed $400M loan to Sunrise Energy signals active policy tailwinds for domestic critical minerals -- a theme worth watching in rare earth and defense-adjacent supply chain names.  Meta's release of Muse Glimmer -- a 30B-parameter, single-GPU model under a permissive open-source license -- is a direct competitive shot at closed-model incumbents and mirrors the open-weight playbook pioneered by DeepSeek and Alibaba. By commoditizing capable edge-deployable inference, Meta is structurally pressuring the enterprise software monetization assumptions underpinning high-multiple AI pure-plays while simultaneously deepening its own platform ecosystem moat through agent-layer adoption.  COMMODITY  Gold consolidating above $4,300 -- well clear of the $4,000 psychological support reclaimed in recent weeks -- reflects a meaningful structural shift in the bullion bid: Friday's jobs miss drove a 0.4% dollar selloff that reinforced the move, CFTC data shows managed money longs at a six-month high, Chinese ETF inflows are on their longest streak since March, and the PBoC extended its now 21-consecutive-month accumulation run with 640,000 oz added in July. With the Fed increasingly split on hikes and CPI the next key pivot, gold's positioning and flow backdrop argues for treating dips as structurally supported rather than reversion opportunities.  Europe's fifth major heat wave of 2025 is tracking toward near-40°C peaks in northern France by Tuesday, with the heat dome blocking moisture replenishment for the Rhine, Po, and Danube -- rivers already at record low navigational levels -- creating a compounding drag on industrial throughput, power generation, and agricultural logistics at the worst possible moment for the continent's supply chains.  Crude is catching a geopolitical bid on holiday-thinned liquidity (Singapore out), with products outperforming crude on the direct refinery hits -- the Jazan drone strike and continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian refining capacity tighten the crack spread narrative near-term. The Iran-Oman navigation lane framework is a technical workaround, not a Hormuz resolution: with no U.S.-Iran direct talks, hardliners consolidating institutional control in Tehran, and CENTCOM actively enforcing the blockade, the full reopening preconditions (naval withdrawal, sanctions relief, war compensation) remain entirely off the table. Treat any "deal is close" headlines as noise rather than a structural oil supply catalyst.  FLOWS AND POSITIONING  Dealer gamma positioning remains deeply constructive for realized vol suppression, creating a mechanical mean-reversion cushion that limits the damage from modest drawdowns this week. The asymmetry, however, is skewed toward the downside: with systematic funds (vol control, CTAs) offering little incremental buying power and skew having already compressed sharply post-Aug 4th, the path of least resistance is sideways-to-lower if any catalyst nudges vol higher -- the offset being accelerating buyback flows as companies exit blackout windows following the near-complete earnings season.  FLOWS REGIME ANALYSIS  Regime: Coiled  The regime shifts from Fragile to Coiled, a meaningful upgrade driven by the closing window of weakness and the continued reinforcement of long gamma conditions. The window of weakness is closing, removing the amplification risk that defined the prior read, and dealers remain firmly long gamma, a level that continues to suppress realized volatility and enforce mean-reversion around the current range. SPX probable volatility bands sit at all-time highs with resistance near 7800 and support near 7600, and critically, the lower end of that range remains well above the gamma flip point, meaning even a near-term dip stays within the stabilizing dealer hedging regime. Put/call skew has compressed sharply following the easing in geopolitical tensions and the fading of earnings event risk, flattening the vol surface across tenors and reducing the structural demand for downside protection. The corporate bid is the emerging bullish catalyst: with 88% of S&P 500 companies having reported, blackout windows are lifting and buyback activity is set to accelerate, introducing a mechanical equity demand flow that was largely absent over the past two weeks. Systematic flows offer little incremental buying power this week, and the asymmetry from that corner remains skewed toward selling into any vol spike, but the corporate bid reloading beneath a long gamma dealer positioning regime is exactly the kind of structural setup that builds coiled energy. The critical overhang is Wednesday's CPI print, which arrives as the focal point for Fed rate path expectations following Friday's payroll contraction that pushed September hike odds lower. Geopolitical risk in crude remains structurally unresolved: the Iran-Oman navigation deal addresses traffic management only, Tehran's core demands are nowhere near the table, and weekend drone and missile strikes on refinery infrastructure keep the energy risk premium alive, meaning a hot CPI could reignite oil-driven inflation anxiety and fracture the current calm.  Cross-Asset Divergence: Aligned -- credit spreads are stable and the dollar holds a stable bid, both consistent with the equity setup's coiled character, confirming that cross-asset stress is not accumulating ahead of Wednesday's data.  Positioning: Lean long on dips within the 7600-7800 range, using the accelerating corporate bid and closing weakness window as the structural anchor, but size conservatively into Wednesday's CPI given the energy inflation overhang and the Fed's fractured internal stance.  Invalidation: A hot CPI print that reignites oil-driven inflation anxiety, pushes yields higher, and begins to widen credit spreads would flip the read back toward Fragile or Risk-Off. Alternatively, a geopolitical escalation that breaks crude sharply higher before the data would remove the current vol compression rationale and challenge the coiled setup.

text: Bessent Remarks on Iran  On August 13, 2026, Bessent said in an interview on Newsmax’s “Rob Schmitt Tonight” that the U.S. will apply measures on Iran “like have never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country.” He added: “Watch this space for more announcements coming next week.”  He specifically described it as “a combination of economic isolation like the world has never seen before, and the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz that will keep anything from going in or out of the Iranian ports.”  This fits into the broader Trump administration strategy of heavy economic pressure on Iran (often referred to in earlier comments as “Operation Economic Fury” or similar efforts), layered on top of existing sanctions, secondary sanctions threats, and the naval/port blockade related to the Strait of Hormuz. The comments come amid ongoing tensions involving Iran, energy flows through the Strait, and efforts to increase pressure without (or alongside) further military escalation.  Major outlets including Reuters, U.S. News, Times of Israel, Arab News, and others reported the statements on the same day. text: US Close | August 10, 2026  The S&P 500 slipped 0.06% to 7,753.12. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 2.94%, and SOXL lost about 7.3%. WTI settled at $82.13 after a 5% jump, while the ten-year Treasury yield reached 4.70%. The broad index barely moved. Semiconductor beta did.  What changed?  Confidence in an early Strait of Hormuz reopening faded as Iran and the US attached compensation and other conditions to a deal. Crude repriced the delay. Fed funds futures put the chance of a September hike back near 52%, up from about 44% after Friday's payroll loss.  Oil was only part of the rates move. The Treasury market also faced $125 billion of new issuance this week. The ten-year yield rose about 4 basis points to 4.701%, and the two-year reached roughly 4.24%. Inflation risk hit the front end while supply leaned on the long end.  Why did chips take the hit?  Nvidia fell 2.9%. Reuters reported that a group including Apollo and Blackstone was working with Nvidia on a funding package of up to $500 billion for AI infrastructure. The funding ambition grew while its cost moved higher.  Intel lost 4.1% after announcing plans to raise $15 billion through a share sale. Dilution gave the semiconductor unwind a company-specific leg. The SOX closed at 11,993.86, just below 12,000.  This was not evidence that AI capex had stopped. It was a crowded group absorbing higher oil, a higher discount rate and Intel supply after a sharp rebound last week.  Why did the S&P hold?  Earnings kept the damage contained. About 85% of the 436 S&P 500 companies that had reported beat estimates, according to LSEG data. Energy shares gained with crude, offsetting part of the pressure in technology, real estate and utilities.  The Nasdaq still had 2,841 decliners against 1,928 advancers. Selling ran wider than the 0.32% index decline, but it never became an index-level liquidation.  What reaches Korea?  Monday's Korean session had already split. The KOSDAQ rose 6.97%, while Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell 0.43% and 0.14%. Foreign investors sold KRW 1.489 trillion on the main board and bought the KOSDAQ.  Tuesday now receives the opposite US semiconductor signal. The first test is foreign cash flow in Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. If those sales persist while equipment names hold, the rotation from memory megacaps into lighter supply-chain beta remains intact.  The demand tape is firmer than Monday's chip prices. TSMC's July revenue grew 44.7% from a year earlier, and the Nvidia financing talks point toward more infrastructure funding. Price is carrying the positioning adjustment before the spending data breaks.  Tomorrow  CoreWeave and Lumentum report after Tuesday's close. Both calls begin at 5 p.m. ET. They can test cloud capacity, optical demand and the cost of financing the buildout.  US July CPI follows Wednesday at 8:30 a.m. ET. Reuters expects headline inflation of 3.4% from a year earlier. Watch whether WTI stays above $80, the ten-year holds 4.70%, and the SOX recovers 12,000. Those three prices decide whether Monday was a one-day leverage reset or the start of a wider discount-rate move.

text: $VLO $MPC $PSX $DINO Hydrocarbon Infrastructure at War: Refinery Outages, Storage Damage and Read-Throughs. New: 8/10/26.  The global refining system is operating under a stress profile that the physical damage statistics alone significantly understate. Effective unavailable capacity — accounting for precautionary shutdowns, utility failures, and logistical disruption alongside direct hardware damage — is materially higher than the percentage of physically impaired assets would suggest. That distinction is critical for understanding why refined product markets are tighter than a facilities-damage assessment implies.  Russia's refining deficit is the most structurally persistent supply disruption in the current environment. Repeated strikes on secondary conversion units — the catalytic crackers and hydrotreaters that upgrade atmospheric distillate into higher-value products — have created a production gap that simple crude throughput restoration cannot address. Secondary unit repair timelines are measured in months to years, not weeks, and the combination of sanctions-constrained equipment sourcing and ongoing strike risk makes restoration timelines genuinely uncertain rather than merely delayed. The practical effect is a persistent Russian middle distillate shortfall that cannot be quickly reversed regardless of how the broader conflict trajectory evolves.  The Gulf region disruption is structurally different — a multifaceted shock affecting crude production, export terminal operations, and shipping route availability simultaneously. Each layer compounds the others: reduced crude availability limits refinery throughput globally, export terminal disruption concentrates the supply shock geographically, and shipping route displacement increases voyage costs and transit times in ways that create effective supply tightness beyond the production volume impact alone.  Middle distillate crack spreads at record levels are the price signal reflecting the specific product mix consequence of these disruptions. Diesel and jet fuel are disproportionately affected because secondary conversion capacity — exactly what has been most damaged in Russia — is what converts atmospheric crude fractions into middle distillates at scale. The global refining system cannot easily substitute for that lost conversion capacity in the near term regardless of crude availability.  Inventory drawdowns are the cumulative financial expression of the supply-demand imbalance, and declining inventory levels reduce the buffer that typically moderates price volatility during supply disruptions. A structurally tight market with low inventories and constrained restoration timelines is the condition that sustains elevated crack spreads rather than normalizing them — and the repair complexity, sanctions constraints, and ongoing conflict dynamics suggest that restoration will be slower and less complete than historical disruption recovery patterns would predict.
